newsitem.title: USA: WHEAT - U.S. export sales pace seen slowing.
newsitem.headline: WHEAT - U.S. export sales pace seen slowing.

text.p: U.S. wheat export sales have been running at a breakneck pace in the early 1996/97 marketing year, but analysts said Tuesday that won't last much longer.

"For the months of June, July and August, the main competitors that we have -- the EU and Canada -- were completely out of the market," said Charlie Sernatinger, vice president of Chicago grain sales for Man International. "They felt that their end-of-season stocks were below pipeline levels."
Joe Christopher, a wheat analyst at LFG in Kansas City, said a good percentage of the U.S. export book to date was built in late spring, when prices were "astronomical and going higher all the time."
"A lot of people -- knowing there weren't any other available stocks in the world -- came here and booked out ahead a little and got some coverage," Christopher said.
"We also ran the (May/July) inverse to a record high and forced a lot of people to cancel April/May commitments and move them into June, and so we had a big June/July book," Christopher said.
But analysts said U.S. dominance of export sales has already started to shift as competitors such as Europe, Australia and Argentina head toward near-record wheat harvests.
"Only in the month of September have the Europeans begun to become sellers and they're only selling for November forward," Sernatinger said. "The Canadians started shipping aggressively this month."
Christopher predicted that U.S. wheat export business will "drop off considerably" in coming months as European and Canadian exports resume.

Bill Tierney, Kansas State University extension economist, said current U.S. wheat export commitments as a percentage of total projected exports represents "one of the largest sales as a percentage of annual as of this date."
Tierney said that as of last Thursday, 1996/97 U.S. wheat export commitments of 566 million bushels constituted 64 percent of his projection for total 1996/97 wheat exports of 885 million bushels.
That compares to a 20-year average of 52 percent for the same mid-September period.

Tierney based his projected total 1996/97 U.S. wheat export figure on USDA's September wheat export estimate of 925 million bushels, except that he subtracted 40 million bushels for wheat products such as flour.
"The USDA does not provide a separate projection for product and grain, so I had to guesstimate product since export commitment figures...are for grain only," he said.
Tierney said he calculated export commitments of 566 million bushels by adding export inspections to date plus undelivered sales as reported in last Thursday's USDA export inspection report.

Turning to wheat by class, Tierney said hard red winter wheat export commitments as of Thursday were 188 million bushels -- about 77 percent of his projection of total HRW wheat exports of 245 million bushels.
His calculated ratio of 77 percent compares to an average HRW wheat ratio of 51 percent over the last 20 years.
Tierney's ratio for soft red winter wheat export commitments versus total projected SRW wheat exports was also 77 percent, compared to the 20-year average of 66 percent.
The ratio for dark northern spring wheat was 58 percent, compared to the average of 49 percent.
Evidence of current tightness in winter wheat supplies can be seen in the most recent data on Kansas City Board of Trade deliverable wheat stocks.

The KCBT said Tuesday that as of September 20, there were 6.564 million bushels of deliverable wheat stocks in the Kansas City area, a little more than half of the 11.743 million bushels in deliverable position a year ago.
